headline: Democrats win control of both parts of Congress

sources.title: 2026 Senate midterm election results as Democrats win control (CBS News)
2026 election: Democrats win full control of Congress (NPR)
Midterms 2026 results and latest updates (Yahoo News)

chunks.text: The United States held [[midterm elections]] on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Midterms take place [[halfway]] through a president's four-year [[term]]. Congress, which writes the country's laws, has two parts, the House of Representatives and the Senate. Each member holds a seat. Every House seat and about a third of Senate seats were [[on the ballot]]. Before the election, Republicans [[controlled]] both parts, but they could not {{hang on to}} either one. Democrats won both and will {{take over}} in early January 2027.

verbs.correct: To keep something you already have
verbs.wrong: To join a group for a short time
verbs.why: Good teams hang on to their best players. Some families hang on to old photos for many years. Republicans could not hang on to either part of Congress.
A new manager takes over the store in June. Big companies often take over small ones. Democrats won both parts of Congress, and they will take over in early January 2027.

chunks.text: The Associated Press, a [[news agency]], had called both parts of Congress for Democrats by the next morning. To call a race means to [[announce]] the winner once the result is clear. Democrats [[flipped]] seven Senate seats. That means they {{picked up}} seats Republicans held, in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine. They will {{end up with}} [[at least]] 54 of the 100 seats.

verbs.correct: To win something you did not have before
verbs.wrong: To count the votes a second time
verbs.why: Popular shows pick up new fans every week. Small parties sometimes pick up a few seats in a close vote. In the Senate, Democrats picked up seven seats that Republicans held before.

verbs.wrong: To ask for something in writing
verbs.why: Many people end up with more books than shelves. Shoppers often end up with things they do not need. Democrats will end up with at least 54 of the 100 Senate seats.

chunks.text: On November 6, votes were still {{coming in}} from [[close races]] in Mississippi and Alaska. In the House, Democrats won far more than the 218 seats needed for a [[majority]], or more than half. Democrats also won several races for [[governor]], a state's leader. One result {{stood out}}. Georgia [[elected]] the first Black woman governor of any US state.

verbs.correct: To arrive, as news or results do
verbs.why: Test results come in a few days after the exam. Phone orders come in all day at the pizza shop. On November 6, votes were still coming in from two close Senate races.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice as special
verbs.wrong: To be argued about in court
verbs.why: A red car stands out in a parking lot full of gray ones. Her voice stands out in the school choir. One governor race stood out because Georgia elected the first Black woman governor of a US state.

chunks.text: President Donald Trump stays in office for two more years, but the other party will control Congress. This is called [[divided government]]. Democrats can {{hold up}} the president's choices for [[judges]] and [[top jobs]], which the Senate must {{sign off on}}. They can also {{look into}} the government's work through [[investigations]]. Trump said he would work with Democrats but would not {{hold back}} from using his [[veto]], his power to stop a bill. Under Senate rules, Democrats do not have the 60 votes needed to {{push through}} most bills over objections.

verbs.wrong: To choose someone for a job
verbs.why: Heavy snow holds up flights at the airport. Missing papers often hold up a new passport. Democrats can hold up the president's choices for judges and top jobs.

verbs.correct: To give official approval to something
verbs.wrong: To write a short note about something
verbs.why: The boss signs off on every new hire. Parents sign off on each school trip. The Senate must sign off on the president's choices for judges and top jobs.

verbs.correct: To study the facts about a problem
verbs.wrong: To hold a vote on a new law
verbs.why: Police look into every report of a stolen car. Doctors look into the cause of a strange illness. Democrats can look into the government's work through investigations.

verbs.correct: To stop yourself from doing something
verbs.wrong: To ask others for their opinion
verbs.why: Shy students often hold back from asking questions. Some buyers hold back from spending when prices rise. Trump said he would not hold back from using his veto.

verbs.correct: To get a law passed when others are against it
verbs.wrong: To write a new law for just one state
verbs.why: Mayors sometimes push through new taxes that many voters dislike. A city council sometimes pushes through a plan that many people dislike. Democrats do not have the 60 Senate votes needed to push through most bills.

mainIdea.s: Democrats won control of the House and the Senate in the November 2026 midterms. The president now faces divided government, and the new majority can slow his choices for judges.
mainIdea.why: Democrats will take over Congress in January 2027. They can hold up the president's choices for judges and top jobs, which the Senate must sign off on.

mainIdea.s: Democrats took both parts of Congress and now hold enough Senate votes to pass almost any bill. The president can no longer stop their new laws because his veto power is gone.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Democrats do not have the 60 Senate votes needed to push through most bills. Trump still has his veto and said he would not hold back from using it.

mainIdea.s: Several states changed their rules for counting mail ballots before voting started in 2026. Election officials hope the new rules help results arrive faster in future contests.
mainIdea.why: This is about who won Congress, not about new counting rules. Democrats picked up seven Senate seats and won far more than 218 House seats.

lines.text: Did you follow the midterm results? [[It's official]]. Democrats won the House and the Senate.
I saw that. So they'll {{take over}} Congress in January?
Right. Republicans couldn't {{hang on to}} either part.
Democrats {{picked up}} seven seats that Republicans held before.
[[In other words]], they flipped seven seats. Even Texas?
Even Texas. They'll {{end up with}} at least 54 seats, and votes are still {{coming in}} from Mississippi and Alaska.
They won way more than 218 seats. A few races are still being counted.
Georgia. Voters there [[made history]] by electing the first Black woman governor of a US state.
So what does all this mean for President Trump?
It's [[a whole new ballgame]]. Democrats can {{hold up}} his choices for judges, since the Senate has to {{sign off on}} them.
Can Democrats pass their own bills now?
Not easily. They don't have 60 votes to {{push through}} most bills, and he said he won't {{hold back}} on vetoes.
Then both sides will need to find [[common ground]].
Well, he did say he would work with Democrats.

expressions.def: Used to say the same thing in a simpler way

expressions.def: Did something important that nobody did before
ex: She made history as the first woman to lead the team.

expressions.def: A situation that is completely different from before
ex: Working from home is a whole new ballgame for me.

expressions.def: Ideas or interests that two sides share
ex: My parents rarely agree, but they find common ground on food.
The two teams looked for common ground before the deal.
